title: Query syntax versus method syntax (two spellings of LINQ)
hook: Language Integrated Query (LINQ) lets you filter and transform collections with either SQL-like keywords or chained method calls. The C# compiler rewrites both spellings into the same method calls — there is no performance difference.

blocks.text: LINQ is a set of operators and language clauses that query any sequence implementing IEnumerable<T> or IQueryable<T>. You can write queries in two styles: query syntax (from … where … select) or method syntax (a chain of .Where, .Select, and similar extension methods). The compiler translates query syntax into method calls. Both styles produce the same deferred execution plan. Creating a query does not touch the source data — execution waits until you enumerate or call an immediate operator like Count or ToList.

entries.plainDefinition: A C# feature that lets you write queries over collections using either keyword syntax or method chains.
entries.example: from row in rows where row.Score > 50 select row.Name

entries.plainDefinition: SQL-inspired keywords (from, where, select, join) that the compiler rewrites into method calls.
entries.example: from x in items where x.Active select x.Name

entries.plainDefinition: A chain of extension methods like Where, Select, and OrderBy on a sequence.
The loop variable introduced by from (e.g., row in rows). It is in scope for where and select.
entries.example: from row in rows — row is the range variable

blocks.text: Knowing both spellings lets you read any LINQ code and choose the style that is clearest. Query syntax puts the range variable first (from row in rows), which is the opposite of SQL's SELECT-first order — a common source of confusion. Method syntax is required for operators that have no keyword equivalent: Count, Any, ToList, ElementAt, and SelectMany overloads with an index. In interviews, saying query syntax is "SQL" or faster than methods is a red flag. The real decision is readability.

blocks.title: When interviewers ask which style to use
blocks.body: Say: "They compile to the same thing. I use query syntax for multi-clause joins and groupings, and method syntax when I need operators without keywords or index overloads."

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Obtain a source
items.body: Start with any IEnumerable<T> or IQueryable<T> — an array, List, or database query.

items.title: Build a query (deferred)
items.body: Write query or method syntax. The compiler rewrites keywords to Where, Select, GroupBy, Join, and SelectMany calls. No data is read yet.

items.title: Execute the query
items.body: foreach, ToList, Count, First, or any immediate operator runs the plan against the current source.

diagram.title: Query syntax compiles to method syntax
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[Query syntax\nfrom x in xs\nwhere p\nselect f] --> B[C# compiler]
  B --> C[Method syntax\nxs.Where(p).Select(f)]
  C --> D[IEnumerable plan]
  D --> E[foreach / ToList / Count]
  E --> F[Results]

snippet.label: Same filter, both spellings
snippet.explanation: let becomes an extra Select with a transparent identifier. Both variables store a deferred plan — neither runs until you enumerate.

snippet.label: Mixing query syntax with method-only operators
snippet.explanation: Parenthesize the query expression, then call .Count(). This is the standard pattern when you need an operator with no keyword.

snippet.label: Nested from becomes SelectMany
snippet.explanation: Two from clauses in query syntax always translate to SelectMany. group … by … becomes GroupBy; join … on … equals … becomes Join.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming query syntax talks to a database because it looks like SQL — it runs on whatever IEnumerable or IQueryable source you gave it. Writing SELECT-first SQL order in C# and expecting it to compile. Believing one spelling is faster than the other. Forgetting that let adds an extra projection step.

blocks.text: Query syntax is pure compiler rewrite to extension methods — identical Intermediate Language (IL) to method syntax for the same operators. Neither spelling changes **iterator allocations**: each deferred operator still allocates a delegate and an enumerator object (or struct enumerator boxed when returned as IEnumerable<T>). The let clause introduces an extra Select and transparent identifier, adding one iterator layer. For hot CSV import paths, method syntax is often preferred because reviewers see the chain and Count/ToList boundaries clearly. How to prove it in production: dotMemory allocation timeline showing WhereIterator + Func delegate per chained operator; BenchmarkDotNet query syntax versus method syntax on the same pipeline — expect parity.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Multi-clause joins and groupings read cleanly
Parentheses required; same IL as methods

snippet.label: Decompile-equivalent — same chain both ways
snippet.explanation: Interviewers asking which is faster expect you to say neither — the compiler rewrites query syntax to the same extension method calls and iterator types.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming query syntax is faster or hits SQL directly — it is compiler sugar over the same IEnumerable/IQueryable operators. Saying let is free — it adds a projection iterator. Insisting one style is always better — senior answer is readability and operator availability. Strong answer: same IL, choose by clarity, method-only for Count/TryGetNonEnumeratedCount, measure iterator allocations on hot paths.

interviewTakeaways: Query syntax translates to method calls; no performance difference — same deferred iterator chain.
from is first so the range variable is in scope — unlike SQL SELECT-first.
let adds an extra Select iterator — not free on hot paths.

60s: Query and method syntax compile to the same operators and same iterator allocations. Use query for joins/groups; methods for Count and operators without keywords. Neither talks to SQL unless the source is IQueryable.
Follow-up: what IL or allocation difference would you expect between the two spellings?
commonPitfalls: Assuming query syntax talks to a database because it looks like SQL — rejected; source type determines execution.
Strong answer: IEnumerable runs in process; IQueryable builds expression trees — spelling is irrelevant.
Believing one spelling is faster than the other — BenchmarkDotNet shows parity for equivalent chains.
Forgetting that let allocates an extra projection iterator in the deferred chain.

jsTsCorrelations.note: rows.filter(...).map(...) is method syntax. JavaScript has no query-expression compiler. Each Array method usually returns a new array immediately — eager — unlike LINQ's deferred Where.
TypeScript has no from/where/select compiler pass. LINQ query syntax is C#-specific sugar; TS always uses method chains on arrays or lazy iterables.
